sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The report analyzes New Zealand Year 5 students from TIMSS 2014/15, with schools sampled separately for Year 5 and Year 9 to minimize overlap. Within New Zealand, classes were sampled with equal probability and all Year 5 students within sampled classes were selected. Exclusions at the New Zealand level are described as: very small schools (fewer than four Year 5 students), special education schools, the Correspondence School, and schools providing more than 50% of instruction in te reo Māori; within-school exclusions include special education classes, special needs students, students with insufficient instruction in English, and units providing more than 50% instruction in te reo Māori. The report also states a general international guideline that countries should keep excluded students to a maximum of 5% of the target population.

data.outcome_summary: This TIMSS 2014/15 Science Year 5 national report summarizes New Zealand’s science achievement and contextual factors using the TIMSS middle primary (Year 5) assessment framework. The assessment is a pencil-and-paper test administered in two timed sessions (36 minutes each) with multiple-choice and constructed-response items, aligned to three science content domains (life, physical, Earth science) and three cognitive domains (knowing, applying, reasoning). New Zealand participated with 6,321 Year 5 students from 167 schools (October–November 2014), and the report describes TIMSS sampling and exclusion rules (e.g., very small schools, special education settings, and te reo Māori instruction thresholds). Achievement is reported on a TIMSS science scale (mean 500, SD 100) with equating across cycles and international benchmarks (advanced 625, high 550, intermediate 475, low 400). The report finds New Zealand’s mean science achievement in 2014/15 was similar to 20 years earlier, higher than 2010/11, and discusses curriculum appropriateness, equity (advanced vs below-low performers), and associations with home resources, school climate, and teacher confidence. It is descriptive and benchmark-based rather than an ML predictive modeling study, so no model performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/R²) are reported.
